claim: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) present specific activation pathways and signaling among receptor subtypes.
source: G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) present specific activation pathways and signaling among receptor subtypes.
evidence: This is a general statement about GPCRs presented in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: A negligible number of drugs have been approved for the adenosine A1 receptor (A1R).
source: Here, we target the adenosine A1 receptor (A1R), for which a negligible number of drugs have been approved.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction discussing A1R therapeutic potential and clinical trial failures.

claim: The A1R activation pathway reveals hidden intermediate and pre-active states together with the inactive and fully-active states observed experimentally.
source: The A1R activation pathway reveal hidden intermediate and pre-active states together with the inactive and fully-active states observed experimentally.
evidence: This claim is supported by metadynamics simulation data presented in Figure 1D-E showing multiple conformational states.

claim: The protein energy networks successfully unravel the extra and intracellular allosteric centers and the communication pathways that couple them.
source: The protein energy networks computed throughout these conformational states successfully unravel the extra and intracellular allosteric centers and the communication pathways that couples them.
evidence: This is supported by the PEN analysis results shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The allosteric networks are dynamic, being increased along activation and fine-tuned in presence of the trimeric G-proteins.
source: We observe that the allosteric networks are dynamic, being increased along activation and fine-tuned in presence of the trimeric G-proteins.
evidence: This is demonstrated through comparative PEN analysis across different conformational states and in the presence/absence of G-proteins (Figures 3, 5, and 8).

claim: Biomolecules present intrinsic dynamism and plasticity to respond to physiological changes.
source: Biomolecules present intrinsic dynamism and plasticity to respond to physiological changes (Wodak et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wodak et al., 2019.

claim: In transmembrane receptors, the binding of ligands in the orthosteric site can establish dynamic and chemical communication with the intracellular region resulting in key structural rearrangements that trigger a particular response.
source: In transmembrane receptors, the binding of ligands in the orthosteric site located at the extracellular region can establish dynamic and chemical communication with the intracellular region resulting in key structural rearrangements that trigger a particular response (Nussinov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nussinov et al., 2014.

claim: Allosteric modulators are capable to bind regions other than orthosteric sites and propagate communication networks to other functional regions of the receptor.
source: Allosteric modulators are capable to bind regions other than orthosteric sites and propagate communication networks to other functional regions of the receptor (Dokholyan, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dokholyan, 2016.

claim: Allosteric drugs offer the advantage of higher selectivity respect to conventional drugs due to the greater sequence variability of allosteric sites.
source: However, allosteric drugs offer the advantage of higher selectivity respect to conventional drugs due to the greater sequence variability of allosteric sites. (May et al., 2007; Christopoulos, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to May et al., 2007 and Christopoulos, 2002.

claim: In G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), the binding of endogenous agonist in the orthosteric site reshapes the conformational ensemble of a Transmembrane (TM) helix to prime the binding and activation of G-proteins.
source: In G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs), the binding of endogenous agonist in the orthosteric site reshapes the conformational ensemble of a Transmembrane (TM) helix to prime the binding and activation of G-proteins. (Erlandson et al., 2018; Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Mafi et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Erlandson et al., 2018; Weis and Kobilka, 2018; and Mafi et al., 2022.

claim: The conformational landscapes of GPCRs associated with the receptor activation are complex, with some general principles in common and also receptor-specific differences.
source: The conformational landscapes of GPCRs associated with the receptor activation are complex, with some general principles in common and also receptor-specific differences. (Bostock et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bostock et al., 2019 and Zhou et al., 2019.

claim: For many GPCRs, inactive and pre-active states are in dynamic equilibrium in the apo form.
source: For many GPCRs it has been observed that (1) inactive and pre-active states are in dynamic equilibrium in the apo form
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Bostock et al., 2019; Mattedi et al., 2020; Miao and McCammon, 2016; Fleetwood et al., 2021.

claim: The action of the agonist induces subtle population shifts involving the stabilization of intermediate and pre-active states and/or decreasing their rates of interconversion in GPCRs.
source: (2) the action of the agonist induce subtle population shifts involving the stabilization of intermediate and pre-active states and/or decreasing their rates of interconversion
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Bostock et al., 2019; Mattedi et al., 2020; Miao and McCammon, 2016; Fleetwood et al., 2021.

claim: The combined action of both agonist and G-protein binding stabilizes a more rigid fully-active state in GPCRs.
source: (3) the combined action of both, agonist and G-protein binding stabilizes a more rigid fully-active state. (Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Bostock et al., 2019; Mattedi et al., 2020; Miao and McCammon, 2016; Fleetwood et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Bostock et al., 2019; Mattedi et al., 2020; Miao and McCammon, 2016; Fleetwood et al., 2021.

claim: The adenosine A1 receptor (A1R) is a member of the class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) family that preferentially couples with Gi/o proteins.
source: The adenosine A1 receptor (A1R) is a member of the class A G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) family that preferentially couples with Gi/o proteins.
evidence: This is established knowledge about A1R classification and coupling preference.

claim: A1R is widely distributed in multiple organs mediating a variety of physiological processes, including those in the brain and the heart.
source: It is widely distributed in multiple organs mediating a variety of physiological processes, including those in the brain and the heart.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deb et al., 2019.

claim: A1R has significant therapeutic potential in the treatment of numerous diseases and disorders.
source: Thus, A1R has significant therapeutic potential in the treatment of numerous diseases and disorders. (Deb et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deb et al., 2019.

claim: A1R has been targeted for pain management through allosteric modulation although without success in clinical trials.
source: In fact, it has been targeted for the pain management through allosteric modulation although without success in clinical trials. (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Bruns and Fergus, 1990)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Draper-Joyce et al., 2021 and Bruns and Fergus, 1990.

claim: X-ray crystallography and Cryo-electron microscopy captured A1R in an inactive and active states revealing a notorious inward-to-outward conformational transition of TM6.
source: Fortunately, X-ray crystallography and Cryo-electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) captured A1R in an inactive and active states revealing a notorious inward-to-outward conformational transition of TM6 (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1). (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Draper-Joyce et al., 2018; Glukhova et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies and shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The most recently released active state structure of A1R is resolved with adenosine, trimeric G-protein and also with a positive allosteric modulator (PAM) located in an extrahelical region.
source: The most recently released active state structure is resolved with adenosine, trimeric G-protein and also with a positive allosteric modulator (PAM) located in an extrahelical region. (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Draper-Joyce et al., 2021.

claim: Computational and mutagenesis studies have reported interesting insights about the A1R activation and allosteric modulation identifying important residues for the signaling efficacy of agonists and cooperativity of PAMs.
source: Computational and mutagenesis studies have reported interesting insights about the A1R activation and allosteric modulation identifying important residues for the signaling efficacy of agonists and cooperativity of PAMs. (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2016b; Do et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Nguyen et al., 2016b; and Do et al., 2022.

claim: A detailed characterization of the allosteric networks that drive receptor activation and G-proteins binding in A1R is still missing.
source: Despite all these achievements, a detailed characterization of the allosteric networks that drive receptor activation and G-proteins binding is still missing.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Either starting from the inactive or active structures, the complete TM6 Inward-to-Outward transition is not sampled in conventional MD simulations.
source: Either starting from the inactive or active structures the complete TM6 Inward-to-Outward transition is not sampled (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cMD simulation data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: When starting from the active structure, an intermediate state centered at ca. TM6 torsion (–140°) and TM3-TM6 distance (15 Å) coordinates is substantially populated.
source: However, when starting from the active structure, an intermediate state centered at ca. TM6 torsion (–140°) and TM3-TM6 distance (15 Å) coordinates is substantially populated.
evidence: This is observed in the cMD simulation data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: When starting from the inactive structure, the receptor mostly samples inactive conformations exhibiting a low probability to progress towards the intermediate state.
source: In contrast, when starting from the inactive structure, the receptor mostly samples inactive conformations exhibiting a low probability to progress towards the intermediate state, thus suggesting a higher inactive-to-intermediate transition time scale.
evidence: This is observed in the cMD simulation data and represents an inference about transition timescales.

claim: The FEL in presence of adenosine confirms that A1R presents three major states in dynamic equilibrium (inactive, intermediate and pre-active).
source: The FEL in presence of adenosine confirms that A1R presents three major states in dynamic equilibrium (inactive, intermediate and pre-active) while the fully-active Cryo-EM like state is not significantly populated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the metadynamics simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The fully-active Cryo-EM like state is not significantly populated in the FEL of A1R in presence of adenosine.
source: The FEL in presence of adenosine confirms that A1R presents three major states in dynamic equilibrium (inactive, intermediate and pre-active) while the fully-active Cryo-EM like state is not significantly populated.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the metadynamics simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The most stable state of A1R in presence of adenosine is the inactive state, followed by the pre-active and intermediate states.
source: The relative stabilities of the three states shows that the most stable state is the inactive, followed by the pre-active and intermediate states, which are slightly higher in energy.
evidence: This is determined from the free energy landscape shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The inactive state of A1R resembles the inactive X-ray coordinates showing short TM3-TM6 distances and low TM6 torsion values.
source: The inactive state resembles the inactive X-ray coordinates showing short TM3-TM6 distances and low TM6 torsion values (state 1 in Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with X-ray structure and shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The inactive conformations of A1R are stabilized by a tight energy coupling between TM3 and TM6.
source: The inactive conformations are stabilized by a tight energy coupling between TM3 and TM6 (see below).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural analysis and further supported by PEN analysis discussed later.

claim: As A1R activation progresses, TM6 torsion evolves further than the TM3-TM6 distance.
source: As the activation progresses, TM6 torsion evolves further than the TM3-TM6 distance.
evidence: This is observed in the metadynamics simulation trajectory analysis.

claim: The remaining energy coupling between TM3 and TM6 ends hampers the progression of the TM6 outward transition during A1R activation.
source: At this point, the remaining energy coupling between TM3 and TM6 ends hampers the progression of the TM6 outward transition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation data based on energy network analysis.

claim: The tug of war between forces provokes the adoption of a torsion in the TM6 end that is signature of the intermediate conformations of A1R.
source: This tug of war between forces provokes the adoption of a torsion in the TM6 end that is signature of the intermediate conformations (state 2 in Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is observed in the metadynamics simulations and shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The pre-active state of A1R presents similar TM3-TM6 distances to the fully-active Cryo-EM structure but exhibits higher TM6 torsion values.
source: The pre-active state presents similar TM3-TM6 distances to the fully-active Cryo-EM structure. However, it exhibits higher TM6 torsion values (state 4 in Figure 1D–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparison with Cryo-EM structure and shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The coupling of the G-proteins is required to stabilize the adoption of the fully-active Cryo-EM like structure of A1R.
source: All together suggest that the coupling of the G-proteins is required to stabilize the adoption of the fully-active Cryo-EM like structure (see next sections).
evidence: This is inferred from the metadynamics results and confirmed by subsequent cMD simulations with G-proteins.

claim: The analysis of the PEN associated with the A1R-ADO ensemble shows that the extracellular region can communicate with the intracellular region through multiple energy pathways.
source: The analysis of the PEN associated with the A1R-ADO ensemble shows that the extracellular region can communicate with the intracellular region through multiple energy pathways (see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In the extracellular region of A1R, ECL2 and ECL3 present a center of communication connecting with TM4, TM5, TM1, and TM6.
source: In the extracellular region, ECL2 and ECL3 presents a center of communication connecting with TM4, TM5, TM1, and TM6.
evidence: This is identified through PEN analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TM6 is energetically coupled with the extracellular region through ECL3/ECL2 and with the intracellular region through TM3 in A1R.
source: TM6 is then energetically coupled with the extracellular region through ECL3/ECL2 and with the intracellular region through TM3.
evidence: This is identified through PEN analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The TM3 end plays a central role for the allosteric communication in the intracellular region of A1R.
source: In fact, the TM3 end plays a central role for the allosteric communication in the intracellular region.
evidence: This is identified through PEN analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: R1083.53 is a communication hub in A1R forming a hydrogen network with D2296.30, D1043.49 (ionic-lock micro-switch) and D326C-Ter.
source: Specifically, R1083.53 is a communication hub forming and hydrogen networking with D2296.30, D1043.49 (ionic-lock micro-switch) and D326C-Ter.
evidence: This is identified through PEN analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Adenosine samples a wide range of poses in its large binding site in A1R.
source: Regarding the energy communication at the orthosteric site, adenosine samples a wide range of poses in its large binding site (Draper-Joyce et al., 2021; Miao et al., 2018)
evidence: This is observed in the simulations and supported by citations to Draper-Joyce et al., 2021 and Miao et al., 2018.

claim: Adenosine performs transient interactions with many residues of the PEN in A1R, establishing multiple transient energy communications that propagate towards the TM6 intracellular end.
source: performing transient interactions with many residues of the PEN, thus establishing multiple transient energy communication that propagates towards the TM6 intracellular end (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation data and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the inactive PEN of A1R, the extracellular ECL2 center is only connected to the intracellular region through TM2 and TM1.
source: We started the analysis with the inactive PEN, which shows that the extracellular ECL2 center is only connected to the intracellular region through TM2 and TM1.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the inactive intracellular region of A1R, R1083.53 establishes a tight communication with D1043.49, D2296.30, and D326C-Ter.
source: In the intracellular region, R1083.53 establish a tight communication with D1043.49, D2296.30, and D326C-Ter, see Figure 3A–B.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: D2296.30 can also communicate with R1053.50 in the inactive state of A1R.
source: Note that D2296.30 can also communicate with R1053.50.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The hydrogen-bonded network that captures the ionic-lock micro-switch is signature of the inactive in-ward conformation of TM6 in A1R.
source: This hydrogen-bonded network that captures the ionic-lock micro-switch is signature of the inactive in-ward conformation of TM6.
evidence: This is inferred from the PEN analysis and structural comparison.

claim: D2296.30-R1083.53 interaction is pivotal to attain the inactive conformation of A1R.
source: In fact, D2296.30-R1083.53 interaction is pivotal to attain the inactive conformation of the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the PEN analysis showing this interaction is key in the inactive state.

claim: D326C-Ter plays an important role in the energy communication of A1R.
source: Interestingly D326C-Ter plays an important role in the energy communication.
evidence: This is identified through PEN analysis across different states.

claim: The flexible C-Ter region can partially occupy the G-proteins binding site and perform stable communication with R1083.53 in A1R.
source: The flexible C-Ter region can partially occupy the G-proteins binding site and perform stable communication with R1083.53.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation data and PEN analysis.

claim: In the intermediate ensemble of A1R, the extracellular communication center is reduced and ECL2/ECL3 region is connected to the intracellular region through TM7 and TM1.
source: We followed the analysis with the PEN of the intermediate ensemble. In this case, the extracellular communication center is reduced and ECL2/ECL3 region is connected to the intracellular region through TM7 and TM1.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The communication through TM6 starts to take place partially in the intracellular region in the intermediate state of A1R.
source: Interestingly, the communication through TM6 start to take place partially in the intracellular region.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the intermediate ensemble of A1R, D2296.30 mainly communicates with R1053.50 instead of R1083.53 in the intracellular region.
source: In contrast with the inactive ensemble, D2296.30 now mainly communicates with R1053.50 instead of R1083.53 in the intracellular region, see Figure 3A–B.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The dynamics of the ionic-lock is altered in the intermediate state of A1R.
source: Therefore, at this point the dynamics of the ionic-lock is altered.
evidence: This is inferred from the change in D2296.30 communication partners between inactive and intermediate states.

claim: The transient D2296.30-R1053.50 interaction is key to prevent TM6 opening after the tension generated in the last segment of TM6 and provokes a torsion in the TM6 intracellular end that captures the receptor in an intermediate state.
source: This transient interaction is key to prevent TM6 opening after the tension generated in the last segment of TM6 and provokes a torsion in the TM6 intracellular end that captures the receptor in an intermediate state (described above).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the PEN analysis with the structural observations from the FEL.

claim: In the intermediate state of A1R, R1083.53 communicates with D422.37 and D1043.49.
source: In this scenario, R1083.53 communicates with D422.37 and D1043.49.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The C-Ter does not communicate with TM3 in the intermediate state of A1R.
source: Note that the C-Ter does not communicate with TM3, which explains the transience of this interaction due to the C-Ter flexibility.
evidence: This is observed in the intermediate state PEN analysis and explained by C-Ter flexibility.

claim: In the pre-active ensemble of A1R, the extracellular ECL2 networks are recovered and connect to the intrahelical region through multiple pathways, including TM2, TM4, TM5, TM6, and TM7.
source: Finally, in the pre-active ensemble, the extracellular ECL2 networks are recovered and connect to the intrahelical region through multiple pathways, including TM2, TM4, TM5, TM6, and TM7.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The PEN captures Y2005.58 and Y2887.53 in the TM5 and TM7 pathways in the pre-active state of A1R.
source: Interestingly, the PEN capture Y2005.58 and Y2887.53 in the TM5 and TM7 pathways, respectively.
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Y2005.58 and Y2887.53 have been found to stabilize the active state of A1R through a hydrogen bond coordinated by a bridging water molecule in the water-lock.
source: These tyrosine residues have been found to stabilize the active state through a hydrogen bond coordinated by a bridging water molecule in the so-called water-lock.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the water-lock mechanism in GPCRs.

claim: The water-lock bridge is not observed in the PEN because non-protein molecules are excluded in the PEN calculation.
source: However, the water-lock bridge is not observed because non-protein molecules are excluded in the PEN calculation, which points out a major limitation of the methodology.
evidence: This is a methodological limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The partial TM6 communication observed in the intermediate state of A1R progresses further in the pre-active state, capturing the toggle switch (W2476.48) and linking with TM5.
source: Regarding the TM6 pathway, its partial communication observed in the intermediate state progresses further capturing the toggle switch (W2476.48) and it is completed linking with TM5 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is identified through state-specific PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The enhanced communication between the intra and extracellular region in the pre-active state is driven by the complete opening of TM6.
source: This enhanced communication between the intra and extracellular region is driven by the complete opening of TM6.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between TM6 opening and enhanced PEN connectivity.

claim: The TM6 opening provokes the break of the ionic-lock disconnecting TM6 (D2296.30) from TM3 (R1083.53 and R1053.50) in A1R.
source: As expected, the TM6 opening provokes the break of the ionic-lock disconnecting TM6 (D2296.30) from TM3 (R1083.53 and R1053.50).
evidence: This is observed in the pre-active state PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: The R1083.53 node loses prominence in the intracellular region in the pre-active state of A1R.
source: Indeed, the R1083.53 node loses prominence in the intracellular region.
evidence: This is observed in the pre-active state PEN analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: R1083.53 can still communicate with D326C-Ter in the pre-active state of A1R, which may compensate the break of TM3-TM6 ends.
source: However, R1083.53 still can communicate with D326C-Ter, which may compensate the break of TM3-TM6 ends (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is observed in the pre-active state PEN analysis and represents a hypothesis about functional compensation.

claim: Among the allosteric residues captured in the PEN of A1R, most of them are identified in the pre-active ensemble while only some of them are identified in the inactive and intermediate states.
source: It is worth mentioning that among the allosteric residues captured in the PEN most of them are identified in the pre-active ensemble while only some of them are identified in the inactive and intermediate states.
evidence: This is observed by comparing experimentally identified allosteric residues with PEN nodes across states.

claim: The enhanced allosteric communication observed upon A1R activation explains why most allosteric residues are captured in the pre-active ensemble.
source: This is due to the enhanced allosteric communication observed upon activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between activation state and PEN connectivity.

claim: The TM6 in-ward to outward transition reveals that the TM6 allosteric pathway along the receptor is missing in the inactive state, partially formed in the intermediate state and completely established upon the receptor activation.
source: The TM6 in-ward to outward transition reveals that the TM6 allosteric pathway along the receptor is missing in the inactive state, partially formed in the intermediate state and completely established upon the receptor activation.
evidence: This is a summary of the PEN analysis across activation states.

claim: The pre-active state of A1R is characterized by an increased allosteric communication through multiple pathways.
source: Indeed, the pre-active state is characterized by an increased allosteric communication though multiple pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of the pre-active state shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The presence of the slim Gαi2-α5 helix in the A1R intracellular cavity prevents TM6 from sampling intermediate and inactive conformations.
source: The population analysis of the receptor activation shows that the presence of the slim Gαi2-α5 helix in the A1R intracellular cavity prevents TM6 to sample intermediate and inactive conformations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cMD simulation data of the ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A1R-Gi2 displays restrictive conformational dynamics by only sampling one major conformational state.
source: Indeed, A1R-Gi2 displays restrictive conformational dynamics by only sampling one major conformational state.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the cMD simulation data of the ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The conformational state sampled by A1R-Gi2 overlaps with both the pre-active state and the fully-active state corresponding to the active Cryo-EM structure.
source: This conformational state overlaps with both, the pre-active state and the fully-active state corresponding to the active Cryo-EM structure (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by projecting the ADO-A1R-Gi2 ensemble onto the FEL in Figure 4B-C.

claim: The binding of the G-proteins induces a population shift in A1R towards fully-active conformations.
source: Thus, the binding of the G-proteins induces a population shift in A1R towards fully-active conformations, as described previously in other GPCRs (Weis and Kobilka, 2018; Mafi et al., 2022; Bostock et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation data and supported by citations to similar findings in other GPCRs.

claim: The PEN of ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex shows some similarities with the PEN of the pre-active ensemble.
source: The PEN analysis shows some similarities respect to the PEN of the pre-active ensemble (Figure 5).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the PEN of ADO-A1R-Gi2 (Figure 5) with the pre-active PEN (Figure 3).

claim: In both the ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex and pre-active ensemble, TM6 allosteric communication is completed and TM7 presents an important communication pathway connecting the intra and extracellular regions.
source: In both cases, TM6 allosteric communication is completed and TM7 presents an important communication pathway connecting the intra and extracellular regions.
evidence: This is observed by comparing PEN analyses shown in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: The presence of G-Proteins finely-tunes the PEN of A1R by propagating the ECL2 extracellular communication center toward the ECL2 helix, capturing the W15645.37 allosteric residue.
source: However, the presence of G-Proteins finely-tunes the PEN in some aspects: (1) the ECL2 extracellular communication center propagates toward the ECL2 helix capturing the W15645.37 allosteric residue that was not identified in previous PEN analysis
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the PEN of ADO-A1R-Gi2 (Figure 5) with previous PEN analyses.

claim: In the presence of G-proteins, the communication pathways between extra and intracellular regions of A1R are refined to only pass through TM2, TM1, TM6 and TM7 and not use TM4 and TM5.
source: (2) the communication pathways between extra and intracellular regions are refined only passing through TM2, TM1, TM6 and TM7 and not using TM4 and TM5
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: TM7 becomes the major communication pathway in A1R in the presence of G-proteins.
source: certainly TM7 becomes the major communication pathway
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The allosteric residue G2797.44 is captured as an important communication node in A1R in the presence of G-proteins.
source: and another allosteric residue G2797.44 is captured as an important communication node
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The end of the α5 helix of Gαi2 (Gαi2-α5 helix) replaces the C-Ter communication position in A1R upon G-protein binding.
source: (3) as expected, the C-Ter does not communicate with TM3 because the end of the α5 helix of Gαi2 (Gαi2-α5 helix) replaces the C-Ter communication position.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: TM3 (R108) communicates with TM2 (D42) and with Gαi2-α5 helix (D667) in the ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex.
source: As a consequence, TM3 (R108) communicates with TM2 (D42) and most importantly with Gαi2-α5 helix (D667).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: D667 of the Gαi2-α5 helix becomes a communication hub in the intracellular region by connecting with H8 (K294) in the ADO-A1R-Gi2 complex.
source: The latest becomes a communication hub in the intracellular region by also connecting with H8 (K294).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The inclusion of Gαi2 causes TM6 (E229) to communicate with TM5 (R208) in A1R.
source: The inclusion of Gαi2 also causes that TM6 (E229) communicates with TM5 (R208), Figure 5.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the PEN analysis of ADO-A1R-Gi2 shown in Figure 5.

claim: The receptor signaling attains a specific profile of protein energy communication networks triggered by the Gαi2 protein coupling.
source: Thus, the receptor signaling attains a specific profile of protein energy communication networks triggered by the Gαi2 protein coupling.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of PEN profiles with and without G-protein.

claim: Multiple pockets are identified in the upper and lower regions of A1R.
source: We identified multiple pockets in the upper and lower regions of the receptor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the MDpocket analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pockets in A1R can change their shape and frequency of formation along different conformational states.
